sweep_summary: Only one title-keyword item exists for Gilbertese: Blevins & Harrison 1999 'Trimoraic feet in Gilbertese' (OL 38(2): 203-230), the catalog's deciding primary. It remains paywalled and unreachable by any open route (Unpaywall/OpenAlex/S2 closed, MUSE captcha, no repository copy, no search-engine hit; this search of works with stress in the title did, however, read two open first-hand texts newly downloaded from archive.org: Bingham 1908's dictionary (p. viii, Note 5: accent weakly marked, final syllable as a rule unaccented, two equal accents in long compounds), which refines and supports the catalog's hedged right-edge/non-final coding without superseding B&H, and Trussel 1979's Peace Corps Grammar Handbook (previously an unfetched works still to obtain), which is silent on stress. catalog's classification unchanged; all files and probes.

new_statements.quote: Note 5. In very many words the accent is not very marked. As a rule, the final syllable is not accented. There are exceptions, numbers of which are marked in the dictionary. Many long words have two accents about equal in force, especially compound words.
new_statements.citation: Bingham, Hiram. 1908. A Gilbertese-English dictionary. Boston: American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions.
new_statements.locator: Key to the Pronunciation, Note 5, printed p. viii (p. 12; scanned text l. 342-346)
new_statements.reading: A first-hand, pre-1999 statement that Gilbertese accent is weak and non-final with multiple roughly equal accents in long words. It is consistent with the catalog's right-edge, non-final, iterating analysis (B&H's penultimate-mora loudness peak in every trimoraic foot) and independently supports the weight-sensitive (tentative) coding (accent 'not very marked', cf. Groves 1985 'much more even'), but it gives no syllable/mora-counting rule and was written by a missionary lexicographer, not a phonologist.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check passes: every quoted fragment is verbatim at the stated page in the held carriers (Martinez-Paricio 2013: 249 and fn. 2; Martinez-Paricio & Kager 2021: 49; Groves et al. 1985: 18 sec. 2.6). (2) The classification rests on the right work -- Blevins & Harrison 1999 is the only dedicated analysis of Gilbertese stress and nothing newer or instrumental was found (secondaries through 2021 cite only it and state no acoustic measurements exist) -- but we do not hold it; the rule reaches us through three mutually consistent secondary quotations, so the grade 'quotation carried over second-hand from StressTyp2' and the weight-sensitive (tentative) classification are honest. The hedge is warranted independently (B&H call their contours impressionistic; Groves 1985 reports near-even stress; Golston 2021 reanalyses as pitch accent). sources.citation: Bingham, Hiram. 1908. A Gilbertese-English dictionary. Boston: American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. Key to the Pronunciation, pp. vii-viii.
sources.quote: Note 5. In very many words the accent is not very marked. As a rule, the final syllable is not accented. There are exceptions, numbers of which are marked in the dictionary. Many long words have two accents about equal in force, especially compound words.
sources.locator: Key to the Pronunciation, Note 5, printed p. viii (p. 12)
sources.note: First-hand, pre-Blevins & Harrison observation by the missionary lexicographer: accent is weakly marked, the final syllable is as a rule unaccented (exceptions are marked in the dictionary with an acute after the accented vowel, e.g. U'ti 'louse', A'ai 'four', Kakao'mara), and long/compound words carry two roughly equal accents. No syllable- or mora-counting rule is stated.

sources.locator: Harrison chapter, printed p. 121; also fn. 14 p. 113: 'overlong vowels are not permitted in Gilbertese.'
sources.note: The chapter is a morphological study (the -i intransitive suffix, high-vowel erasure, nasal-final intransitives). The words 'stress', 'accent', 'foot', 'prosody' and 'tone' do not occur in it; no stress placement, secondary stress, domain or exception is stated anywhere in the chapter or elsewhere in the volume for Gilbertese. The one prosodic remark is a trimoraic minimal-word condition on nouns and verbs standing alone in their phrase ('trimoric contentive lengthening'), which is consistent with the catalog's mora-counting statement but is not a stress description. Nothing on tone.
